prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

By menopause, it’s not just estrogen my mother lacks. She’s lost her eldest son— that’s me, the one who’s queer—the doctor who once made her very proud. These days, I do my own wash when I’m home, I cook for her so she can take a break from all the chores she now refuses to assign to me. She sits, half-watching Ricki through her tea’s thin steam, her squint of disapproval more denial than it is disgust. She hears much better than she sees—it’s easier to keep out vision than it is to clear the air of sounds—and yet I know it’s age that stultifies her senses too. Enraged because she’s lost so much, I understand why suddenly she looks so stunned as from the television: “. . . Bitch, she stole my boyfriend, my own mother did! . . .” I fold a towel noiselessly. I know she thinks it’s garbage, sinful, crap—just as she thinks that taking estrogen in pills is not what God intended, no matter what the doctors say; or that I’m gay is plain unnatural, she can’t endure such pain. The oven timer rings. The cookies that I’ve baked are done. I’ll make another batch though she won’t touch them: given up for Lent. My mother’s love. I wonder where it went.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: She, These, Ricki

outputs.L1: By menopause, it is not only estrogen my mother lacks. She has lost her eldest son—that is, me, the one who is queer—the doctor who once made her so proud. outputs.L2: At menopause, estrogen is not the only thing my mother has been deprived of. She has also lost her firstborn son—me, the queer one—the physician who used to fill her with pride. Now, when I visit, I launder my own clothes and make meals for her so she can rest from the household tasks she no longer lets herself give to me. She sits there, only partly watching *Ricki* through the faint vapor rising from her tea, her narrowed look suggesting refusal more than revulsion. Her hearing is far sharper than her sight—it is simpler to shut out what one sees than to empty a room of sound—though I also know that age has dulled all her perceptions. Furious over everything taken from her, I can see why she suddenly appears so shocked when the television declares, “. . . Bitch, she stole my boyfriend, my own mother did! . . .” I quietly fold a towel. I know she considers the show trash, wickedness, filth—just as she believes that swallowing estrogen tablets goes against God’s design, whatever physicians may claim; and that my being gay is simply against nature, a sorrow she cannot bear. The timer on the oven goes off. The cookies I made are ready. I will bake more, although she will not eat any of them: she has given them up for Lent. My mother’s affection. I ask myself where it disappeared.
outputs.L3:
The speaker portrays his mother as a woman overwhelmed by grief, anger, and confusion. She mourns what she sees as the loss of her eldest son—not because he has died, but because he is queer. In her mind, his sexuality has transformed him into someone she can no longer recognize or accept. This grief is made even more painful by the memory of who he used to be in her eyes: a successful doctor, a son who once made her proud. The contrast between her former pride and her current rejection reveals the depth of the emotional rupture between them.

Despite this rejection, the speaker continues to care for his mother in practical, intimate ways. He does her laundry, cooks for her, and tries to make her daily life easier. These acts of service show his enduring love and sense of responsibility, even though she resists depending on him. Her reluctance to accept his help suggests both pride and discomfort. She may need him, but accepting care from the very son she struggles to accept forces her to confront feelings she would rather avoid.

The mother’s disapproval extends beyond her son’s sexuality. She objects to television, estrogen pills, and anything that seems to represent moral decline, bodily change, or a departure from the values she holds dear. Her reactions are rooted in religious belief, but they also reveal a deeper difficulty with change. The world around her has shifted, and so has her family, in ways she cannot control. Her faith becomes both a source of certainty and a barrier that prevents her from fully seeing or embracing her son.

As she ages, the mother appears increasingly burdened by accumulated losses. Time, disappointment, and grief have left her stunned and angry. Instead of softening, she has become emotionally distant, as though the weight of what she has endured has made it difficult for her to offer tenderness. Her inability to respond warmly to her son is not presented as simple cruelty, but as part of a larger portrait of someone who has been hardened by age, sorrow, and fear.

For the speaker, however, understanding his mother’s pain does not erase his own. Her rejection wounds him deeply. He continues to love and care for her, but he is left asking what became of the love she once had for him. The central sadness of the relationship lies in this unanswered question: how can a mother’s pride and affection turn into grief and disapproval simply because her child reveals who he truly is? The speaker’s pain comes from living in that contradiction—still reaching toward his mother, even as she pulls away.
outputs.L4:
He comes to visit his mother in the late afternoon, when the apartment has already begun to dim and the television has been speaking for hours to no one in particular. Its sound fills the rooms with weather reports, commercials for medicine, a preacher’s voice rising and falling between promises of salvation, a game show audience applauding as if joy could be manufactured on schedule. His mother sits in her chair with a blanket over her knees, small inside the furniture now, her hands folded in a way that reminds him of church: obedient, waiting, almost severe.

She does not rise when he enters. She says his name, but not with surprise or warmth. It is more like an acknowledgment that something expected has happened. He kisses her cheek anyway. Her skin is soft and papery, carrying the faint smell of lotion, talcum powder, and the soup she reheated earlier but did not finish. For a moment, he feels the old reflex of love move through him before memory interrupts it.

He asks if she has eaten. She says she has. He checks the kitchen and finds the bowl in the sink still half full, the surface of the broth filmed over with grease. He does not correct her. Instead, he rolls up his sleeves and begins to wash the dishes.

The apartment holds evidence of her decline in small, accusing ways. Dust gathers along the window ledge beneath the framed photograph of his parents on their wedding day. Pill bottles crowd the counter beside a plastic cup. A stack of unopened mail leans against the toaster. The trash needs taking out. A basket of laundry sits beside the hallway, clean but unfolded, as if she had made it halfway through the task and then been defeated by the thought of sleeves, towels, socks.

He moves from room to room quietly, doing what needs to be done. He wipes the counters. He throws away expired food. He changes the sheets on her bed, tucking the corners tightly because she likes them that way, because he remembers her teaching him how to make a bed when he was a child. He remembers her hands then—quick, capable, warm. He remembers her singing hymns while she worked. He remembers the way she once bent over him when he had a fever, pressing a cool cloth to his forehead and calling him her sweet boy.

Now, when he returns to the living room with the laundry basket, she watches him with an expression he cannot read. Suspicion, perhaps. Or sorrow. Or the stubborn composure of someone who has decided not to ask questions because she fears the answers and already believes she knows them.

On the television, a man in a suit is speaking about sin. His mother does not reach for the remote. Neither does he.

“Do you want me to turn this down?” he asks.

“It’s fine,” she says.

But it is not fine. The room is full of judgment, though no one has said anything directly. That is how it has been between them for years: not silence exactly, but avoidance arranged into the shape of conversation. She asks whether he is working too much. He asks about her medication. She says the neighbor’s daughter is pregnant again. He tells her the pharmacy changed its hours. They speak in practical fragments, stepping around the subject that sits between them like another piece of furniture.

His life has become something she refuses to name. She will say “your friend” instead of “your partner.” She will ask if he is “still living in that place,” as if the apartment he shares with the man he loves is temporary, improper, a mistake that might yet be corrected. She keeps old photographs of him on the wall: school portrait, graduation picture, the version of him in a tie standing beside her after confirmation. She does not display any recent ones.

Once, years ago, he tried to tell her plainly. He had chosen a Sunday afternoon because he thought the day might soften her. She had been making tea. He remembers the spoon stopping against the cup, the tiny clink that followed. She did not shout. That almost made it worse. She closed her eyes as if receiving bad news from a doctor.

“I will pray for you,” she said.

He had wanted to say, I am not sick. I am not lost. I am standing right here. But her grief had entered the room so quickly that there seemed to be no space left for him. She mourned the son she imagined she had lost while he sat across from her, alive, waiting to be loved.

Since then, her love has not disappeared, exactly. It has changed shape. It has become careful and conditional, buried beneath disappointment and doctrine. She worries whether he is eating, whether he is safe driving at night, whether he has a winter coat. But she will not ask whether he is happy. She will not bless the life he has built. Her concern comes wrapped in denial, and he has learned to accept it in pieces, like food from a table where he is not fully welcome.

Still, he comes.

He comes because she is old now. Because her ankles swell. Because she forgets appointments. Because the woman who once carried him can no longer carry a grocery bag from the car. He comes because love, for him, has not been replaced by judgment. It has been wounded by judgment, made heavier and more complicated, but not erased.

He folds her laundry while the preacher on television warns of the world’s corruption. His mother’s nightgowns are thin from washing. Her towels smell faintly of lavender detergent. He pairs her socks, stacks them neatly, places them in the drawer where she can reach them. These gestures feel both intimate and unbearable. There is tenderness in caring for the body of someone who has refused part of your soul. There is humiliation in it too, and anger, and a strange, persistent mercy.

“Did you talk to your sister?” his mother asks.

“Last week,” he says.

“She worries about you.”

He almost laughs, but he does not. “I know.”

His mother looks toward the television. “We all do.”

There it is: the doorway opening, not enough to enter, only enough to show him the room beyond. Worry. Sin. Shame. Salvation. Words she has arranged around him like bars.

He presses a folded towel flat with both hands. “You don’t have to worry about me.”

She says nothing.

He wants, suddenly and fiercely, to ask what she thinks love is for if it cannot survive the truth. He wants to ask whether all those years in church taught her compassion or only fear. He wants to ask if she understands that he has spent half his life grieving too—not for the son she lost, but for the mother who chose a doctrine over knowing him.

Instead, he carries the towels to the bathroom.

When he returns, she has muted the television. The silence startles him. She is looking down at her hands.

“You don’t have to do all this,” she says.

“I know.”

“I can manage.”

He looks at the full trash bag by the door, the pill organizer he filled for the week, the dishes drying in the rack. “I know,” he says again.

Her mouth tightens. For a second he thinks she might cry, and he feels the old panic of childhood—the fear of his mother’s sadness, the desire to fix it even when he is not the one who broke it. But she only lifts her chin.

“You were always a good boy,” she says.

The sentence lands softly and cruelly. Were. Boy. A version of him preserved in the past, innocent because he was unfinished, lovable because he had not yet spoken.

He sits across from her. The room is nearly dark now except for the blue flicker of the television and the thin gold light at the edge of the curtains. He can see how tired she is. He can see the veins in her hands, the tremor in her fingers, the stubbornness that age has not weakened. He can see, too, that she loves him as much as she is able, and that what she is able to give is not enough.

This is the truth he returns to again and again: her rejection has not made him stop loving her. It has only made love more painful, more deliberate. Each visit is a choice. Each chore is a sentence he cannot say aloud. I am here. I am still your son. I will not become what you fear, and I will not abandon you to your fear either.

Before he leaves, he brings her a glass of water and sets it on the table beside her chair. She thanks him without looking up. At the door, he tells her he will come by next week.

“Drive safe,” she says.

“I will.”

He waits, foolishly, for something more. His name spoken with tenderness. A blessing. An apology. A question about the man waiting for him at home. But she has already turned the volume back on. The preacher’s voice rises again, filling the apartment with certainty.

In the hallway, he stands for a moment before pressing the elevator button. He feels the ache of the visit settle into him, familiar and deep. Behind him, through the closed door, his mother sits among the clean dishes, folded laundry, and muted evidence of care. She may never understand what it costs him to keep coming. She may never see that his tenderness is not weakness or surrender, but a kind of grace she taught him before she began to withhold it.

Then the elevator arrives, and he steps inside, carrying both the hurt of being judged and the quiet dignity of having loved anyway.
outputs.L5:
She stood at the edge of the quiet street, holding a small box tied with blue ribbon. These were the memories she had kept for years: faded photographs, handwritten notes, and a silver key that no longer opened any door she knew.

Ricki had always believed that every object carried a story. When she opened the box, she smiled softly, remembering the laughter, the long walks, and the promises made under summer skies. These moments, though simple, had shaped who she had become.

She closed the box again, not with sadness, but with gratitude. Ricki knew that the past could not be changed, but it could be honored. And with that thought, she stepped forward, ready for whatever came next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem in the voice of a queer eldest son visiting his religious mother during menopause, weaving in domestic chores, daytime TV, estrogen, Lent, and the pain of maternal rejection.
counterfactuals.output:
I come home with a bag of oranges  
and the old key still on my ring,  
though the house has learned to hesitate  
before opening.

Mother is on the couch  
with a blanket over her knees,  
fan turning its slow opinion  
from room to room.  

On the television, women applaud  
a man who has wronged everyone.  
A host in bright lipstick says  
healing is a choice,  
and the audience claps  
like rain on a roof we cannot afford to fix.

I take the laundry from the dryer,  
fold her nightgowns into soft squares,  
pair the socks she buys in bulk  
from the pharmacy.  
In the kitchen, dishes wait  
with their cloudy mouths open.  
I wash each one  
as if forgiveness is a grease  
hot water can lift.

She says her doctor mentioned estrogen,  
says the word like contraband,  
like a girl’s name she once knew  
before marriage, before church hats,  
before my father’s voice  
became the weather.

Her body is changing  
without asking permission.  
At night she burns from the inside,  
wakes damp and furious,  
kicks off the sheet,  
prays for the Lord  
to make her temper mild.

It is Lent.  
On the fridge, a magnet from Nazareth  
holds up a list of things  
she has given up:  
sugar, gossip, soda after noon.  

Not me.  
Never me, exactly.  

Only the version of me  
who came home one spring  
with my voice shaking  
and a man’s name  
held out in both hands  
like an offering.

She did not yell.  
That was the mercy  
and the knife.

She looked past me  
toward the crucifix in the hallway,  
as if I were a stain  
on the wall behind it.  
She said she loved me,  
but not this.  
As if this  
were a coat I could remove,  
hang neatly by the door,  
walk back into the family  
bare-armed and acceptable.

Now I vacuum around her slippers.  
Now I change the sheets  
while she tells me the pastor says  
the world is ending  
in small ways every day.  

I want to say: yes.  
I know.  
A mother can end it  
at the kitchen table  
with a teacup in her hand.  

Instead I ask  
where she keeps the extra trash bags.  
Instead I scrub the bathtub ring.  
Instead I cut an onion  
and let it blame itself  
for my face.

On TV, a cooking show  
turns flour, eggs, and butter  
into something holy.  
My mother dozes,  
one hand open on her lap,  
palm lined and tender  
as an old map.

I remember that hand  
checking my forehead for fever,  
buttoning my school shirt,  
pressing a cross of ash  
over the place  
where my thoughts would grow  
too loud for her.

Eldest son,  
practice child,  
small husband of the house—  
I learned early  
how to carry groceries,  
how to lower my voice,  
how to read silence  
like scripture.

Outside, March is trying  
to become April.  
The trees hold their buds  
tight as secrets.  

In the sink, the last plate  
slips from my soapy fingers  
and does not break.

She wakes and says my name  
the way she used to,  
before it gathered conditions.

For a second,  
I am twelve again,  
standing in the doorway  
with clean hands,  
waiting to be told  
I am good.

Then the show comes back  
from commercial.  
Someone has lost weight.  
Someone has found God.  
Someone’s daughter  
is forgiven on a stage  
under studio lights.

My mother asks  
if I will stay for dinner.

I say yes,  
because hunger is older than pride,  
because love can be  
a chore you return to,  
because the body, even rejected,  
keeps making room  
for breath.

In the kitchen  
I set the table for two.  
Forks on the left,  
knives turned inward,  
water glasses catching  
the late gold light.

I do not bless the food.

I let the steam rise  
between us  
like something neither of us  
knows how to name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary monologue/poem about a gay doctor son caring for his aging mother, who disapproves of his sexuality and refuses hormone therapy, with imagery of laundry, baking cookies, and a Ricki Lake–style talk show in the background.
counterfactuals.output:
I fold your nightgowns like small white flags,  
Mother,  
warm from the dryer,  
each one surrendering its shape  
to my hands.

In the next room the television blooms—  
studio lights, applause, a woman crying  
under the bright tribunal of daytime:  
a Ricki Lake kind of mercy,  
chairs angled toward confession,  
every wound made public enough  
to be forgiven between commercials.

You call it trash.  
You watch it anyway.

I am in your kitchen,  
your son with the careful fingers,  
the doctor’s hands you bragged about  
before you learned what else they loved.  
I measure flour, soften butter,  
press my thumb into dough  
as if taking a pulse.  
The cookies spread on the pan,  
round and golden,  
obedient to heat.

You say no to the pills again—  
no estrogen, no patch, no cream,  
no to the small chemistry  
that might ease the desert in your bones,  
the sleep torn into ribbons,  
the sudden fires beneath your skin.  
You say, I am not putting that in my body,  
as if your body has not already become  
a house full of strangers:  
stairs that betray you,  
joints that lock their doors,  
a heart I listen to through cotton and age  
while you stare past me  
at the host on television  
asking some trembling boy  
when he first knew.

I knew at seven, maybe,  
when I preferred the clean scent of sheets  
to the rough anthem of fathers,  
when I loved the neighbor’s son  
with a terror so private  
I mistook it for prayer.

You knew later.  
Or perhaps you always knew  
and waited for God  
to correct my posture.

Now I change your bedding.  
Now I sort the towels from the darks,  
your stockings from my scrubs,  
your shame from my devotion—  
though the colors bleed, Mother,  
they always do.

You refuse to say my husband’s name,  
but you eat the cookies he taught me to make:  
brown sugar, cinnamon, a little salt  
to sharpen the sweet.  
You close your eyes after the first bite,  
and for one second your face  
is not a verdict.

Onscreen, the audience leans forward.  
Someone’s mother stands up, weeping,  
and says, I don’t understand,  
but I don’t want to lose you.

The applause rises like water.

You ask me to turn it down.  
I do.

I sit beside you with the plate between us,  
your laundry cooling in the basket,  
your body cooling in its long season,  
my stethoscope coiled in my bag  
like a question I no longer ask.

I cannot cure you of time.  
You cannot cure me of myself.

Still, tonight, I lift your feet  
and slide the soft socks over them.  
Still, you let me.  
Still, the cookies breathe sugar into the room.  
Still, the dryer hums its small, domestic hymn,  
turning and turning  
what is damp, what is worn,  
what has been stained beyond naming,  
toward warmth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poignant narrative poem about family estrangement: a mother has “lost” her queer eldest son emotionally, even though he is home doing chores for her. Include menopause, Catholic guilt/Lent, and a final line questioning where her love went.
counterfactuals.output:
In Lent she gives up sugar,  
then salt, then speech—  
sets each small hunger on the sill  
like a votive she expects God to light.

The house is full of him.

Her eldest son bends over the sink,  
his sleeves rolled past the wrists  
she once kissed clean of fever.  
He scrubs the roasting pan,  
takes the bins to the curb,  
lifts the laundry basket  
as if it were no heavier  
than all the names she will not say.

He has come home again  
because the boiler failed,  
because her knees are bad,  
because menopause has turned her nights  
to sudden flame and drenched sheets,  
because she is frightened  
of the body’s betrayals  
and the long hallway after dark.

He changes bulbs, tightens screws,  
finds her glasses where she left them  
beside the statue of Mary,  
blue-robed, immaculate,  
watching everything  
and forgiving nothing out loud.

At dinner, she asks if he wants more potatoes.  
She does not ask about the man  
whose texts light up his phone.  
She does not ask who holds him  
when he is finally held.  
Instead she folds her napkin  
into a little white surrender  
and says the parish is collecting cans.

All through March, ashes fade  
from foreheads in the supermarket.  
She remembers pressing her thumb  
to his baby brow,  
the soft pulse there,  
the priest’s hand pouring water,  
her own proud whisper: firstborn.

Now he moves through the kitchen  
like a guest with keys.  
He knows which drawer sticks,  
which stair complains,  
how she takes her tea.  
He knows not to mention pride,  
or Christmas, or the year  
she said she needed time  
and time became a locked room.

At night she lies awake, burning,  
rosary knotted in her fist,  
counting beads like debts:  
Hail Mary, full of grace,  
what is a mother  
when her blessing turns to blade?

Downstairs, he rinses the last cup,  
sets it to dry,  
turns off the light she always forgets.

She hears the door click softly.  
She tells herself he is still here.  
She tells herself loss is for graves,  
for ships, for coins slipped through floorboards.

But in the dark, her son’s footsteps  
recede inside the house,  
and she knows there are distances  
no car can cross,  
no chore can mend,  
no forty days can cleanse.

She has not lost his hands,  
his shoulders, his dutiful return—  
only the boy who once ran to her  
believing she was home.

And where did her love go?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a confessional poem in a formal, polished style about a gay man’s relationship with his conservative mother; set it in her house while he folds towels, bakes cookies, and overhears trashy TV, contrasting medical knowledge with religious belief.
counterfactuals.output:
In my mother’s house, the towels are squared like flags,  
white terry folded into thirds, then thirds again—  
a discipline she taught me with her hands,  
those chapel hands, ringed, softened now by age.  

The dryer sighs. Beyond the laundry room,  
the television sells its gaudy grief:  
some woman crying under studio lights,  
some man forgiven, damned, exposed by noon.  
My mother lets it thunder through the walls  
while Scripture, framed in gold, outstares the set.  

I smooth each towel along its seam, as though  
a life might be corrected by a crease.  
She calls my name from somewhere near the stove  
and asks if I still keep that “friend” of mine.  
Her voice is mild. The question is a knife  
wrapped in a napkin, set beside my plate.  

I bake her cookies anyway: brown sugar,  
butter beaten pale, vanilla’s ghost  
rising sweetly in the kitchen heat.  
She blesses everything before it enters  
the mouth—bread, broth, the body’s hungers—  
except the hunger that has made me human.  

Once, I tried to tell her what I knew:  
the body is no sermon gone awry,  
no vandal scripture written in the blood.  
Desire blooms through hormone, nerve, and brain;  
the heart conducts its old electric claim.  
There is no stain a microscope can find,  
no shadow on the chromosomes of love.  

She answered with her pastor’s softer wrath:  
We love the sinner. Then she looked away,  
as if my life had dressed indecently  
and stood too near the family photographs.  
Christ watched us from the hallway, pale and still,  
His wounded hands extended toward us both.  

Now evening settles on her curtained rooms.  
The cookies cool. The television laughs.  
I stack the towels in their ordained white towers,  
small linens for the cleansing of the flesh.  
My mother hums a hymn beneath her breath,  
and I, her son, keep measuring the space  
between what heals and what is called a cure,  
between the soul she prays I’ll one day save  
and this poor body, faithful to its truth.  

I do not tell her I have prayed as well—  
not to be changed, but seen; not pardoned, known.  
I do not tell her how a man once touched  
my face as if it were not evidence  
but mercy, ordinary and complete.  
I only lift the warm pan from the rack,  
offer her the first imperfect one,  
and watch her take it gently in both hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic first-person poem that begins with the idea “By menopause, it’s not just estrogen my mother lacks,” and explores a mother’s denial, aging senses, homophobia, and the speaker’s quiet acts of care.
counterfactuals.output:
By menopause, it’s not just estrogen my mother lacks,  
but certain mercies of the body—  
the little oils of patience,  
the softening rain behind the eyes.  

She says she is fine  
while leaving the stove to bloom blue in the kitchen.  
She says she can see  
and squints past my face toward the television’s holy static.  
She says she can hear  
but answers the question she has already forgiven herself for missing.  

All her senses are old dogs now,  
turning in circles before they lie down.  
Taste has gone first—  
she salts the soup until the sea comes back  
and calls it bland.  
Smell follows, a ghost with no forwarding address;  
she cannot tell when milk has soured,  
when smoke has begun its gray sermon  
from the pan.  

Still, she sharpens herself  
on the things she refuses to lose.  
My name, for one.  
The one she gave me, not the one I chose.  
The daughter she made, not the son I did not become,  
not the body I love beside me  
when the world goes dark and ordinary.  

When I tell her I am happy,  
she studies the tablecloth.  
When I say her name,  
my lover’s name,  
she flinches as if I have opened a window in winter.  
She says, Don’t bring that here,  
as if love were a stray animal,  
wet, diseased, nosing at her door.  

And still I come.  
I change the batteries in her remotes.  
I write large labels on the pillbox—  
morning, noon, night—  
as if time itself might be persuaded  
to take her gently.  
I throw out the spoiled fruit before she sees it.  
I lower the flame.  
I stand between her and the smoke alarm’s shriek.  

She denies the cataracts, the ringing,  
the way the house has narrowed  
to a corridor of guesses.  
She denies the years collecting in her joints  
like weather in a closed room.  
She denies me, sometimes,  
with the same mouth that asks  
if I have eaten.  

Mother, I want to say,  
your fear is not faith.  
Your cruelty is not tradition.  
The world did not end  
because I kissed a woman  
and meant it.  

But her hands tremble  
when she lifts the cup,  
and I take it from her  
before the tea can scald her lap.  
I wipe the saucer.  
I fold the towel.  
I let the silence live.  

There are wars  
too small for history  
and too large for one kitchen.  
There are victories  
that look like clipping her nails,  
like reading the instructions aloud,  
like pretending not to notice  
when she forgets the word for spoon.  

At night, I lock her door from the inside,  
test each burner with my palm,  
turn off the lamp she swears she never left on.  
She sleeps in the next room,  
snoring softly, defenseless as a child  
who would never choose me.  

And I, who was not chosen fully,  
choose the orange bottle, the clean sheet,  
the glass of water placed within reach.  
I choose not to answer every wound  
with a blade of my own.  
I choose the care she cannot name,  
the love she cannot bless,  
the daughterhood I carry  
like a basin of fire  
through the darkened hall.
